The hours-long attack spanned six districts of the city, killing one person and wounding at least 16, Ukraine's national police said. It came a day after a Ukrainian drone attack struck e-commerce warehouses near Moscow — the latest exchange in an intensifying summer air campaign. Al Jazeera noted Kyiv is weathering near-daily strikes amid a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors (its best defence against ballistic missiles).
stories.why: Even with a comparatively low death toll, a record ballistic-missile salvo underscores how thinly stretched Ukraine's air defences are as Western interceptor stocks run low.

stories.headline: US mounts seventh straight night of strikes on Iran, broadening targets as Gulf states drawn in
stories.summary: The US mounted a seventh consecutive night of airstrikes on Iran overnight into Saturday 18 July, and by mid-morning declared the wave concluded — while visibly widening its target set beyond military installations. Al Jazeera reported the latest strikes hit bridges and energy infrastructure and cut off water to villages in southern Iran, which its correspondent framed as a broadening of the campaign from narrowly military objectives toward civilian infrastructure. Swiss broadcaster SRF reported that Washington had formally called the seventh strike wave over, even as Iran continues to fire on the Gulf states hosting US forces. The exchange extends an escalation that has drawn US bases across the Gulf into direct fire since the Strait of Hormuz standoff sharpened in June, with both sides publicly rejecting the negotiated pause each accuses the other of refusing.
stories.why: A bombing campaign now in its seventh straight night, reaching bridges, power and water supplies and pulling Gulf states into direct exchanges, raises the risk of a wider regional war and keeps Hormuz shipping and energy markets on edge.

stories.headline: Anyon fusion makes a minimal non-Abelian topological code universal
stories.summary: Topological quantum computing stores information in the collective ("anyonic") excitations of an exotic quantum phase, where operations performed by dragging anyons around one another are intrinsically shielded from local noise. The long-standing catch: the simplest non-Abelian phases cannot produce a complete ("universal") set of quantum operations by braiding alone. This team prepared a 54-qubit ground state of the "quantum double of S₃" — the smallest non-Abelian group — on Quantinuum's H2 trapped-ion processor, then showed that fusing anyons (merging them and reading the outcome), used as an active computational step, supplies exactly the missing ingredient to reach universality. Think of braiding as tying protected knots and fusion as reading which knot you tied: it is the first hardware demonstration that fusion, not just braiding, closes the universality gap for a minimal non-Abelian code.
stories.why: A real machine coaxed the simplest "impossible" topological code into doing the full quantum-computing repertoire — by fusing quasiparticles rather than only looping them.

stories.headline: SEED: Self-Evolving On-Policy Distillation for Agentic RL
stories.summary: Outcome-based RL for long-horizon agents gives one sparse reward at the end of an episode, leaving the "credit assignment" gap: the model gets almost no signal about which intermediate decisions were good. SEED closes it without a separate teacher: the same policy analyzes its own completed trajectories and writes short natural-language "skills" (reusable workflows, decisive cues, failure-avoidance rules), then measures how much conditioning on those skills shifts its own action probabilities. That probability shift becomes a dense, token-level distillation signal trained jointly with ordinary RL — and because the policy is both actor and analyst, the hindsight supervision co-evolves with the model rather than being frozen in a fixed teacher. Across text and vision agentic benchmarks it improves both success rate and sample efficiency with better generalization to unseen tasks.
stories.why: Agents that teach themselves from their own experience, converting vague episode-level rewards into fine-grained, self-generated feedback.

stories.headline: Zelensky sacks defence minister Fedorov, triggering renewed protests in Kyiv
stories.summary: Thousands rallied again in Kyiv on Saturday 18 July against President Volodymyr Zelensky's dismissal of defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, deepening a political crisis that opened when Zelensky sacked him on Wednesday 15 July. Fedorov, 35 — the youngest defence minister in Ukraine's history and the figure most identified with its drone-warfare programme — was removed in a government reshuffle that Le Temps reads as a clash of doctrine between a younger, technology-driven generation and older commanders still shaped by Soviet-era methods. The upheaval lands despite a run of better news for Kyiv: a 90 billion euro EU loan, reinforced backing from the coalition of the willing, and Ukrainian strikes on military and energy sites deep inside Russia.
stories.why: Sidelining the minister most associated with Ukraine's drone edge — while Moscow shows no interest in negotiating — risks fracturing national unity at a moment Kyiv can least afford it.

stories.headline: Moonshot's Kimi K3 is the first open model in the ~3-trillion-parameter range, and it lands near the frontier
stories.summary: K3 is a multimodal open-weight mixture-of-experts model with 2.8 trillion total parameters — activating just 16 of 896 experts per token — a one-million-token context, and native image/video input; full weights are due 27 July. It pairs a new "Kimi Delta Attention" scheme that Moonshot says decodes up to 6.3× faster at million-token contexts. On the independent Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index it scores 57 — level with Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5, behind Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol — and on the GDPval v2 agentic benchmark it jumps to an Elo of 1,668 (from K2.6's 1,190), beating GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.8 but trailing Fable 5. One honest caveat from the same eval: its hallucination rate rose (39% → 51%) even as accuracy improved, so it answers more questions right but also fabricates more. Pricing ($0.30/M cached input, $15/M output) is well above the previous K2.6, which the write-up reads as the end of rock-bottom Chinese frontier pricing.
stories.why: this is the edition's headline. An openly-released model at 2.8T parameters scoring within a few points of proprietary flagships collapses the gap between the open and closed tiers faster than most expected — with direct consequences for anyone (in a sovereignty-conscious region especially) weighing whether they can self-host near-frontier capability rather than rent it. The rising hallucination rate is the asterisk: near-frontier on aggregate scores does not mean near-frontier on factual reliability.

stories.headline: On-device models can be re-tokenized in place to cut decode cost 2–4× for under-served languages
stories.summary: A tokenizer — the fixed table that chops text into the sub-word units a model reads — is frozen at the start of pretraining, and it allocates its vocabulary to whatever languages mattered then. Languages added later get split into many more tokens per word, which directly raises latency, compute and energy for their users. On a big cloud model the token table is a rounding error; on a compact on-device model it is a real share of the per-token cost, so small models ship small vocabularies and accept the fragmentation. This paper's "tokenizer expansion" continues the existing byte-pair-encoding merges (the rule that greedily glues common character pairs into tokens) on a multilingual corpus, so old tokens carry over unchanged and each new token has an exact decomposition into old ones; new embedding rows are initialized as the mean of their parts, then a two-stage retrain recovers quality. Applied to an 8B mixture-of-experts checkpoint (MoE — only a few "expert" sub-networks fire per token), it encodes Hindi and Vietnamese in ~2.4× and ~2.6× fewer tokens (up to 4.0× on Thai), for an estimated 2.2–3.7× per-character decode speedup on those languages.
stories.why: it is a concrete, reader-relevant lever for the local-inference world — the paper describes producing the LFM2.5-8B-A1B model and releasing the weights and expanded tokenizer — and it targets a real equity gap, since the users paying the fragmentation tax are disproportionately non-English speakers on the cheapest hardware.

stories.headline: US strikes reached closer to Tehran than at any point in this war overnight, as Iran claimed retaliatory hits on US bases across the Gulf
stories.summary: US Central Command said it struck command centres, air-defence sites and missile and drone facilities at Bandar Abbas and, in a 90-minute wave late Wednesday, coastal-defence and cruise-missile positions on Greater Tunb Island near the Strait of Hormuz; it also said it disabled a non-compliant oil tanker with Hellfire missiles to enforce a naval blockade reimposed on Tuesday 14 July. Iranian media reported strikes across at least nine locations and a hospital in Ahvaz evacuating 211 patients; Iran's army in turn claimed attacks on US radar and Patriot systems at Ali Al Salem airbase in Kuwait, the Sheikh Isa base in Bahrain and al-Azraq in Jordan, while Jordan said it intercepted eight Iranian missiles. At least 35 people have died and more than 300 been wounded since this wave began around Wednesday 8 July, and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps threatened to halt all Middle East energy exports over the blockade: either for everyone or for no one.
stories.why: A direct US-Iran exchange now straddling the Strait of Hormuz - the chokepoint for roughly a fifth of the world's seaborne oil - with an explicit threat to the region's energy exports is the single most consequential escalation risk on the board, and the first strikes near Tehran mark a widening, not a winding-down.

stories.headline: Ukraine's parliament confirms Naftogaz chief Serhii Koretskyi as prime minister
stories.summary: Koretskyi, who ran the state energy company Naftogaz, was approved with 289 votes; Zelenskyy argued his energy record made him best placed to steer Ukraine through another wartime winter of attacks on the power grid. The vote came as hundreds protested outside parliament against the dismissal of Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov after only six months, with critics warning it could disrupt military reforms mid-war. Overnight, Russia again hit Kyiv with ballistic missiles, killing at least two, according to Ukrainian authorities, while Ukrainian drones struck a residential building in the southern Russian city of Engels on the Volga.
stories.why: A government shake-up at the top of a country under daily bombardment is a real governance risk - the reshuffle trades continuity for Zelenskyy's bet that an energy technocrat can keep the lights on through winter.

stories.headline: US–Iran ceasefire collapses: Washington resumes strikes and Hormuz blockade, Iran hits Gulf bases
stories.summary: US Central Command (CENTCOM — the US military command for the Middle East) said it launched a fresh seven-hour wave of strikes from about 02:00 GMT Wednesday, hitting "dozens of military targets" — missile and drone sites, naval capabilities and coastal defences — near the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow chokepoint through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil passes. Iran's health ministry said more than 260 people were injured and over 30 civilians killed in the latest US attacks, with strikes reported on the port city of Chabahar and a base at Bampur in the southeast. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it struck US military facilities in Bahrain (the home port of the US Fifth Fleet), a logistics centre at Mina Abdullah in Kuwait, and the al-Azraq base in Jordan; Kuwait reported a naval vessel hit and four personnel wounded, and Jordan said it downed four Iranian ballistic missiles. Tehran declared the memorandum of understanding (MoU — the tentative peace framework signed less than a month ago) void, and the IRGC threatened to halt all Middle East energy exports, warning that oil and gas would flow "for everyone or for no one."
stories.why: A signed de-escalation framework has unravelled in under a month into direct US strikes on Iranian soil and Iranian attacks on three Gulf states at once — the widest regional spillover yet, with an explicit threat to global oil supply through Hormuz.

stories.headline: A star found whose orbit could probe the spin of the Milky Way's black hole
stories.summary: For decades, tracking individual stars looping around Sagittarius A* — the 4.3-million-solar-mass black hole at the Galactic centre — has let astronomers weigh it and confirm Einsteinian effects like the gravitational redshift. But those effects scale as (v/c) squared; the black hole's spin only shows up one order deeper, at (v/c) cubed, and no known star orbited fast and close enough to reach it. The GRAVITY team now reports S301, a faint (K-band magnitude 19.3) main-sequence star on an 8.7-year orbit with a small enough closest approach that, with continued monitoring, its orbit becomes sensitive to the spin — the Kerr (rotating-black-hole) correction to spacetime. This is the discovery of a suitable probe, not yet a spin measurement.
stories.why: Measuring a black hole's spin from a star's orbit would be a first, and a stringent new test of general relativity in the strong-field regime right at our Galaxy's heart.
affiliations: Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics
stories.affiliation_label: Observatoire de Paris, Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics

stories.headline: Russia pounds Odesa ports for a fifth day; Ukraine strikes 20 Russian Black Sea vessels
stories.summary: Odesa region governor Oleh Kiper described a "massive" overnight drone-and-missile attack on 14–15 July on civilian, industrial and port infrastructure; three were killed and three wounded in Odesa, with further strikes on the port of Chornomorsk. Russia's defence ministry confirmed hitting the Odesa and Chornomorsk ports, saying it targeted fuel-storage and drone-assembly sites. Kyiv's drone-force commander said Ukraine in turn hit 17 Russian oil tankers, two gas tankers and a tugboat, part of a campaign to disrupt Russian logistics and isolate occupied Crimea.
stories.why: The fighting has concentrated on the Greater Odesa ports that handle most of Ukraine's grain and cargo exports, so the escalation threatens both civilian lives and the wartime economy — and pulls Black Sea shipping lanes further into the war.

stories.headline: A cryogenic strontium tweezer array holds single atoms for two hours
stories.summary: Neutral-atom quantum computers trap individual atoms in optical tweezers — tightly focused laser beams that hold one atom each — and are scaling toward tens of thousands of qubits. The bottleneck is a trade-off: keeping atoms trapped for a long time usually means sealing them inside a cold, cramped enclosure that blocks the optical access the machine needs to manipulate them. This group reports a cryogenically-cooled apparatus that sidesteps the trade-off, holding single strontium-88 atoms in a tweezer array for vacuum-limited lifetimes of up to two hours while preserving full optical access, and without a complex cryogenic shroud. Room-temperature setups typically lose atoms in tens of seconds; a two-hour lifetime means an atom essentially never leaks away during a computation.
stories.why: Longer trap lifetimes translate directly into more qubits held stably at once, so this is a concrete engineering step toward the large atom arrays that error-corrected quantum computing will need.
affiliations: Max Planck Institute of Quantum Optics
stories.affiliation_label: Max Planck Institute of Quantum Optics, LMU Munich

board.headline: US and Saudi strikes hit Iraq militias
board.summary: US and Saudi Arabia carried out joint air strikes on Iran-backed militias in Iraq before dawn on Wednesday 29 July, the first major US military action in the Middle East since President Trump paused a 13-day bombing campaign last Friday (24 July). Iraq's Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF — an umbrella of Iraqi militias trained and backed by Iran, and legally part of Iraq's own security apparatus) said at least 20 of its members were killed and 32 wounded in strikes across several sites. Saudi Arabia and US Central Command (CENTCOM) said the operation targeted militias responsible for drone attacks on American troops and on Saudi oil facilities in the Eastern Province and around Riyadh; Riyadh said it "does not seek escalation" but would respond to aggression. The PMF called the strikes a "highly dangerous escalation" and a violation of Iraqi sovereignty, while the Islamic Resistance in Iraq denied any role in the attacks on Saudi Arabia and called the kingdom's claims "fabrications" — so responsibility for the drone attacks that Riyadh cites as justification is itself contested. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi convened an emergency national-security council meeting and is expected to travel to Saudi Arabia on Thursday 30 July.
board.why: It pulls the Iraqi state into a fight between its own Iran-aligned forces and the US-Saudi axis just days into a fragile pause in the wider Iran war, and risks reigniting a conflict Washington had declared suspended.

board.headline: Kumamoto quake death toll rises to 13
board.summary: The death toll from the magnitude-7.1 earthquake that struck Kumamoto Prefecture on the Japanese island of Kyushu rose to at least 13 confirmed dead on Wednesday 29 July, with five more feared dead and rescuers still searching a collapsed shopping mall. The quake hit Tuesday 28 July at 16:27 local time (07:27 GMT); the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) put it at magnitude 7.1 while the US Geological Survey measured 6.8. At least three of the deaths came at an Aeon shopping mall in the town of Kashima, where a gas explosion after the tremor tore through the building and collapsed a large section, the retailer's president confirmed. A wall of the centuries-old Kumamoto Castle also partly collapsed, and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said the toll was expected to rise as police, firefighters and Self-Defense Forces personnel continued the search.
board.why: It is the deadliest quake to hit Kyushu since the 2016 Kumamoto disaster, and the death toll has climbed sharply from the "at least 50 injured" reported when the tremor first struck.

board.headline: Senate advances Russia sanctions bill
board.summary: The US Senate voted 86-12 on Tuesday 28 July to advance a Russia sanctions bill, a bipartisan procedural step that its sponsors described as largely symbolic ahead of the chamber's August recess. The measure, renamed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026 after the South Carolina senator who died suddenly of an aortic tear, would give the president new authority to sanction Russian officials, foreign nationals and financial institutions tied to Moscow's war effort, compel a 500% tariff on all Russian imports including oil and gas, and expand powers to punish "shadow fleet" vessels evading energy sanctions. Only one Republican, Rand Paul, joined 11 Democrats against it; Graham's sister Darline, appointed to fill his seat, is a lead sponsor. The Senate will need several more votes for the bill to pass, and the House passed its own version in June.
board.why: The lopsided vote signals durable cross-party support for tougher Russia measures, but Tuesday's step authorizes rather than imposes the tariffs — the sanctions are not yet law.

board.headline: Keiko Fujimori sworn in as Peru president
board.summary: Keiko Fujimori was sworn in as Peru's president on Tuesday 28 July for the 2026-2031 term, becoming the country's ninth head of state in a decade and vowing a hardline crackdown on crime. Fujimori, 51, daughter of the late former president Alberto Fujimori (in office 1990-2000, imprisoned for corruption and crimes against humanity), won the 7 June runoff by fewer than 50,000 votes over leftist rival Roberto Sanchez, after losing three previous runoffs. She pledged to deploy the military for "order" in areas hit by gangs, drug trafficking and illegal mining, and floated mass deportation of irregular migrants, anonymous judges, and prison labour in exchange for food. Homicides in Peru rose from about 1,000 in 2018 to 2,600 in 2025, and extortion complaints jumped from 3,200 to 26,500 over the same period.
board.why: Her inauguration marks the return of "fujimorismo" to power in a country worn down by chronic political instability and its worst security crisis in decades.

board.headline: UBS Q2 net profit rises 17 percent
board.summary: UBS reported second-quarter net profit up 17% to $2.8 billion (CHF 2.3 billion) on Wednesday 29 July, with pre-tax operating profit jumping 64% to $3.59 billion. The results, under CEO Sergio Ermotti, come as the bank presses ahead with absorbing Credit Suisse, an integration it expects to largely complete by year-end. The rebound in profitability follows a period dominated by the costs and complexity of the 2023 emergency takeover of its former rival.
board.why: UBS is now Switzerland's only globally systemic bank, and its earnings trajectory feeds directly into the politically charged debate in Bern over how much additional capital the enlarged bank should be forced to hold.

board.headline: Zug funds research on system it pays into
board.summary: The canton of Zug — by far the largest net contributor to Switzerland's inter-cantonal fiscal equalization system (the Finanzausgleich, which redistributes money from wealthy cantons to poorer ones) — is helping fund a new research centre that will critically examine that very system, SRF reported on Wednesday 29 July. Zug's payments into the scheme have climbed to nearly CHF 500 million, and it will contribute several million francs toward building the centre. Lausanne economist Marius Bruelhart welcomed private funding of research in principle but warned the output must be clearly labelled as commissioned work, arguing Zug plainly has expectations about the findings and that genuinely independent research would have been put out to open tender.
board.why: It puts a spotlight on the conflict of interest when the biggest payer into a redistribution system bankrolls the scholarship used to argue for reforming it.

board.headline: Opus 5 tops the ARC-AGI leaderboard
board.summary: On ARC Prize's official scorecard, Claude Opus 5 at maximum reasoning effort scores 97.5% on ARC-AGI-1 and 90.4% on ARC-AGI-2, and is the top model on the newer interactive ARC-AGI-3 at 30.2%. ARC-AGI is a suite of abstract visual-reasoning puzzles deliberately built to resist memorization — you infer a hidden rule from a few examples and apply it — and ARC-AGI-2 in particular was designed to stay hard for frontier LLMs, which makes a 90% figure a notable jump rather than a routine leaderboard nudge.
board.why: ARC-AGI is the benchmark most explicitly aimed at fluid reasoning rather than recalled knowledge, so a frontier model clearing 90% on its second-generation set is a real signal about where reasoning models are — while ARC-AGI-3, still at 30%, marks how far the interactive, multi-step version remains from solved. These are ARC Prize's verified scores on its semi-private set, not a vendor's self-report, which is what makes them worth citing.

board.headline: M7.1 quake strikes southern Japan
board.summary: A magnitude-7.1 earthquake struck southwestern Japan on Tuesday 28 July, hitting Kumamoto prefecture on the island of Kyushu and injuring at least 50 people. The quake struck shortly before 16:30 local time at a shallow depth of about 10 km (roughly 6 miles), according to the US Geological Survey; the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) issued a tsunami advisory for waves of about one metre along the Ariake and Yatsushiro seas and urged people away from the coast. Several thousand homes lost power, rail services stopped, and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi warned of strong shaking around Uki City and Makigawa Town. Japan's Nuclear Regulation Authority reported no abnormalities at nearby nuclear plants. Kumamoto is the same prefecture devastated by a pair of major quakes in 2016.
board.why: Japan sits on the "Ring of Fire" and records roughly a fifth of the world's earthquakes, but a shallow M7.1 directly under a populated region is at the severe end and the tsunami and landslide risk will keep the response tense for days.

board.headline: DeepSeek's MLA splits content from position
board.summary: Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) — the attention variant introduced in DeepSeek-V2 that squeezes the key-value cache through a shared low-rank bottleneck (a compression step that cuts memory ~81% at inference, the main cost of long context) — is now in production models, but nobody had checked what the bottleneck keeps and what it throws away. Training a small 114M-parameter transformer end to end and probing its internals, the authors find the compressed channel learns an almost pure content representation: it retains entity identity (98%) while discarding positional information, which the model reconstructs elsewhere.
board.why: MLA is one of the load-bearing tricks behind cheap long context, copied into models most people now use, yet it was adopted for its memory savings without anyone knowing what it costs representationally. A clean it separates content from position, and here's where position goes is exactly the kind of grounding that lets the next architecture tweak be deliberate rather than superstitious. That the study runs at 114M rather than frontier scale is the honest caveat.

board.headline: Bounding the train-inference gap stabilizes RL
board.summary: When labs fine-tune a model with reinforcement learning (RL — training by reward signal rather than by copying examples), the code that generates candidate answers and the code that updates the weights are usually separate engines, and the generator often runs in lower-precision arithmetic to go fast. That mismatch makes the two disagree about what the model actually said, and past a point the training destabilizes. ACRL (Adaptive Control RL) measures the discrepancy live and keeps it inside a safe band; as a side effect it raises policy entropy, nudging the model to keep exploring rather than collapsing onto one answer.
board.why: RL post-training is now how reasoning models are made, and our run diverged and we don't know why is a common and expensive failure. Naming the training-inference gap as a controllable quantity — not an unavoidable artifact of the systems stack — turns a mysterious instability into a dial.

board.headline: What reward models actually memorize
board.summary: A reward model is the learned judge that scores answers during alignment training — get it wrong and every model trained against it inherits the bias. Measuring counterfactual memorization (how much a specific training pair changed the model versus what it generalized), the authors show reward models misallocate memory to easy, high-margin preference pairs, latch onto dataset-specific shortcuts like which model produced an answer, and over-generalize crude correlates of human preference — longer answers, more compliant tone — when they meet unfamiliar comparisons.
board.why: the model is well-aligned ultimately rests on the reward model judging quality rather than surface features, and this is direct evidence that today's discriminatively-trained judges are not yet doing that in context-dependent cases. It's a caution for anyone treating a reward score as ground truth.

board.headline: RLVR extended to open-ended tasks
board.summary: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) drove much of the recent reasoning-model progress, but it only works where correctness can be checked automatically — arithmetic, unit tests — leaving open-ended writing or dialogue dependent on costly, biased LLM-judges. RLSVR (the S for self-verifiable) borrows a trick from self-supervised learning: it transforms an open-ended task into a proxy task the model can grade itself against (for example, reconstructing a corrupted target), manufacturing a verifiable reward from the data rather than an external judge.
board.why: the biggest limitation on the RLVR recipe is the shrinking supply of tasks with a clean automatic grader. If self-verifiable proxies hold up, that unlocks the same training machinery for the messy majority of tasks where is this good? has no unit test — though whether the proxy actually rewards the quality you care about is the thing to scrutinize.

board.headline: CoT-faithfulness detectors fail where models err
board.summary: A chain-of-thought (CoT) — the written reasoning a model shows before its answer — only supports oversight if it is faithful, i.e. the stated steps actually produced the answer rather than being a plausible after-the-fact story. Auditing black-box detectors of unfaithful CoT against human-annotated data, the authors find answer correctness structures everything: 69% of annotated unfaithfulness happens on wrong answers, and on those wrong answers no tested detector beats chance. Just knowing the answer is wrong (not a deployable signal) outpredicts every purpose-built detector.
board.why: a lot of safety hope rests on reading a model's reasoning to catch when it's being deceptive or shortcutting. This says the reasoning trace is least trustworthy exactly when the model is wrong — the case you most need to catch — which connects to the government-lab finding this week that evaluation-gaming often leaves no trace in the chain-of-thought at all.

board.headline: Consensus decoding blocks fine-tuning backdoors
board.summary: Recent work shows a tiny amount of poisoned fine-tuning data can install targeted misbehavior, and even innocuous-looking data can transmit hidden preferences. Standard defenses (filtering, mixing in clean data, regularization) dampen but don't remove the effect. This paper pursues robustness through redundancy: fine-tune a separate model on each data source, then at generation time combine their next-token predictions with a consensus rule (e.g. a token-wise minimum), so anything only one poisoned source wanted gets suppressed.
board.why: as organizations fine-tune on data scraped or bought from many sources, one bad supplier can backdoor your model is a real supply-chain risk. Consensus-at-decoding is an appealingly simple mitigation — it needs no trust in any single source — at the cost of running several models.

board.headline: KV-cache eviction as an estimation problem
board.summary: A model serving long context has a bounded working memory (the KV-cache — the stored keys and values it attends back over) and must keep deciding which items to drop. Every deployed method — StreamingLLM, H2O, SnapKV — commits the instant an item arrives, guessing whether it'll be reused. This paper recasts the decision as estimating a hidden signal (will this be needed?) and points out the missing middle: fixed-lag smoothing, which waits a bounded number of steps, watches which items a correct near-future prediction actually attended to, and only then commits.
board.why: the KV-cache is the memory wall of long-context serving, and eviction policies are usually hand-designed heuristics. Casting the whole family as points on one axis — how long you wait before committing — is a genuinely clarifying frame, and it suggests a cheap way to approach the unbeatable offline optimum by measuring rather than guessing.

board.headline: Microsoft ships MAI-Cyber-1-Flash
board.summary: Microsoft unveiled MAI-Cyber-1-Flash, a small security model (from its MAI-Thinking-1 line) embedded in its MDASH multi-agent system, plus Perception, an agent that monitors and mitigates threats in real time. The combination scores 96% on CyberGym — a benchmark measuring how well a model finds real security flaws in large codebases — which Microsoft says is 12 points above the Mythos system and ahead of Gemini and GPT; it claims ~50% lower cost because the small model handles 90% of tasks and escalates only the hardest to GPT-5.4.
board.why: the framing is telling — Microsoft positioning itself as an orchestrator routing most work to a cheap in-house model and buying frontier reasoning only when needed is the cheap specialized model below, expensive frontier above pattern showing up across the industry, and a shift for a company whose cloud growth ran on exclusive OpenAI distribution. Every number here is Microsoft's own on a benchmark it selected; independent evaluation is the thing to wait for.

board.headline: Netanyahu and Zelenskyy meet Trump
board.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy both descended on Washington on Tuesday 28 July to meet President Donald Trump, as a long-stalled Russia-sanctions bill neared a Senate vote and the wars in Iran and Ukraine visibly converged. Both leaders were in the US chiefly for the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham, a Trump ally and hawkish backer of both Israel and Ukraine who died on 11 July; Netanyahu was set to meet Trump with the US-Israel war on Iran topping the agenda, while Zelenskyy pressed for anti-ballistic-missile defences and help producing Patriot systems. The sanctions bill Graham championed would impose 100% tariffs on the five largest buyers of Russian oil and gas - including China and India - and Trump has moved at the last minute to fold sanctions on Iran into the same package. The convergence is concrete: Ukraine attacked an Iranian tanker in the Caspian Sea on Saturday 25 July that it says was ferrying drones and components to Russia, Iran has vowed to retaliate, and Russia said more than 390 Ukrainian drones struck the Moscow region overnight. Trump has said talks with Iran are under way during the current pause in US strikes.
board.why: Two wars 2,500 km apart are being wired together through Washington's sanctions machinery and Iran's arms pipeline to Moscow - treat both leaders' framing as advocacy, since each is seeking Trump's backing.

board.headline: Seoul's Kospi plunges 10.8%
board.summary: South Korea's Kospi stock index collapsed 10.8% on Tuesday 28 July, closing at 6,023.66 - its lowest since April - after a rout in chipmaking shares triggered trading circuit-breakers (automatic pauses meant to halt panic selling). Samsung Electronics sank 13.4% and SK Hynix 14.7%; together the two account for a large share of the Seoul market. The sell-off followed a report in the trade publication The Information that China has begun mass-producing homegrown deep-ultraviolet (DUV) lithography tools - the machines that print circuit patterns onto silicon wafers, and a capability Western and Korean firms had assumed China was years from matching - stoking fears that Chinese competition could erode the incumbents' lead. European markets opened slightly higher, suggesting the shock stayed largely regional for now.
board.why: Semiconductors are the backbone of South Korea's export economy, so a one-day drop this steep is a real macroeconomic event - and it signals investors are newly worried that China's chip progress could reset a market the West has dominated.

board.headline: Wildfires push 300,000 from homes near Bordeaux
board.summary: Wildfires around Bordeaux drove one of the largest evacuations in French history, with around 300,000 people now moved to safety across France and Spain and the flames roughly 15 km from the city. In southwest France the fire in the Gironde has burned more than 19,000 hectares and destroyed about 100 buildings since Wednesday, forcing some 220,000 people from their homes — 55,000 more ordered out around Bordeaux over the weekend, and 31,000 in neighbouring Landes; boats were used to evacuate holidaymakers from the Cap Ferret peninsula. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the blaze turned "extremely violent and unpredictable" overnight, the A63 motorway to Spain is shut over about 60 km, and nearly 100,000 hectares have burned nationwide since January — a historic record. In Spain the government declared a state of emergency around Madrid and in Ávila (where about 47,000 hectares burned), with roughly 90,000 people evacuated according to the interior ministry; El País reports the Madrid, Ávila and Toledo fires have covered some 77,000 hectares in all. A new heatwave with temperatures up to 40°C is forecast from Tuesday 28 July, threatening to worsen the fight.
board.why: This is the sharp escalation of a fire emergency running across France, Spain and Italy since 23 July — the direct threat to Bordeaux, a metropolis of about 850,000, and the incoming heat push it well beyond the earlier evacuations.

board.headline: Pogacar equals all-time Tour record
board.summary: Slovenia's Tadej Pogacar (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) sealed his fifth Tour de France on the Champs-Elysees, drawing level with the sport's four all-time greats - Jacques Anquetil, Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault and Miguel Indurain - as the only riders to win cycling's biggest race five times. It is his third in a row. As flagged here last week, the contest had effectively closed once his one real threat, two-time winner Jonas Vingegaard, abandoned with a broken collarbone on stage 15; his other rival, Belgium's Remco Evenepoel, finished second overall, 6 minutes 26 seconds back. Pogacar, 27, took five stage wins including a record ascent of Alpe d'Huez.
board.why: Five wins puts Pogacar in the conversation as the greatest cyclist ever - but the reception is telling. He was booed by some fans during the race, less out of dislike than frustration that his dominance has drained the Tour of suspense. That tension - a generational champion whose brilliance makes the event less competitive - is now the sport's central question.

board.headline: Iran vows retaliation over Caspian Sea strike
board.summary: Iran warned Ukraine it will retaliate for a deadly strike on an Iranian commercial vessel in the Caspian Sea, opening a new front that links the Russia–Ukraine war to the recent US–Israel conflict with Iran. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday 26 July that the Ukrainian attack the day before — which Iran says caused the ship to explode, killing one sailor and injuring several — "cannot go unanswered" and violated the UN Charter, and he accused Israel of provoking it to "drag Europe into its war." Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his forces had hit "vessels used in military cargo shipments involving Iran, as well as a warship" in long-range strikes, and accused Russia of feeding Iran satellite imagery of US facilities in the Gulf. Iran has summoned Ukraine's chargé d'affaires in Tehran, and a senior lawmaker said early Monday that Kyiv "may soon come to understand that Iran does not let actions go unanswered." Separately, the United States and Iran held off on fresh strikes for a second straight day, and oil prices eased.
board.why: Kyiv striking an Iranian ship — over Tehran's supply of Shahed drones to Moscow since 2022 — risks pulling Iran directly into the Ukraine war just as a fragile pause in the US–Iran fighting takes hold.

board.headline: Berlin Pride attacker shot dead by police
board.summary: German police shot dead the suspect in Saturday night's Berlin Pride van-ramming attack, which Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said authorities are treating as an "Islamist terrorist attack." The suspect was killed in a police operation on Sunday 26 July after, police said, attacking officers with a bladed weapon; Dobrindt said there was no indication of a further threat. One person was killed and 29 injured — a higher toll than the 16 reported the day before — when the attacker drove a van into a crowd in Tiergarten Park, near the Christopher Street Day parade, one of Europe's largest LGBTQ+ celebrations. Chancellor Friedrich Merz urged marchers "not to be intimidated," and the Brandenburg Gate was lit in the colours of the Pride flag for a candlelit vigil.
board.why: The "Islamist terrorist" classification is the interior minister's characterisation and the investigation is early, but a deadly attack on a Pride event has already prompted German calls for tighter security.

board.headline: Swiss Super League season opens
board.summary: The 2026-27 Swiss Super League - the country's twelve-team top flight - kicked off this weekend, and the two marquee Sunday fixtures both turned on late comebacks. In front of a sold-out St. Gallen, the hosts trailed to a first-half Umeh Emmanuel goal for Zurich before Lukas Goertler equalised from a worked corner (70') and summer signing Andrin Hunziker deflected in the winner four minutes later for a 2-1 St. Gallen victory. It was a pointed result for FCZ's new coach Marcel Koller - the man who led St. Gallen to their last league title 26 years ago - whose reshaped side created the better first-half chances but left empty-handed. In Bern, Young Boys threw away a 2-0 lead against Sion before Samuel Essende's second-half brace rescued a 4-2 win.
board.why: For most Swiss towns the Super League - not the World Cup that just finished - is the sport that structures the autumn, and the opening weekend already hints at the season's shape: a champion (Thun) nobody expected to defend, a rebuilt Zurich under a returning veteran coach, and a St. Gallen side punching above its weight at home and in Europe.

board.headline: Norris wins as Antonelli leads title
board.summary: Lando Norris won the Hungarian Grand Prix for his and McLaren's first victory of the 2026 season - a striking line to write about a team that dominated the sport a year ago. His race-long McLaren team-mate Oscar Piastri led the first half after passing Norris at the start, but lost time trapped behind a Carlos Sainz-Fernando Alonso battle (Sainz got a five-second penalty for ignoring blue flags and drifting into Piastri, who raged over team radio), was overcut by Norris in the pits, then retired with a gearbox failure on lap 56. Max Verstappen salvaged second from a difficult weekend; Mercedes' teenager Kimi Antonelli took third after Lewis Hamilton was demoted by a pit-lane speeding penalty.
board.why: A year ago McLaren were the benchmark and Antonelli a rookie; that a Mercedes driver now leads by two clear wins' worth of points, and McLaren celebrated its first win only in late July, is the clearest sign yet that the 2026 regulation reset genuinely reshuffled the grid rather than merely tweaking it.

board.headline: Tagger and Halys land maiden titles
board.summary: The post-Wimbledon lull is a quiet, lower-tier stretch of the calendar, but this week delivered two genuine breakthroughs. Austrian teenager Lilli Tagger won the WTA Prague Open for her first career title on the women's tour, beating Ukraine's Daria Snigur 7-6(3), 6-2 on Sunday. A day earlier, France's Quentin Halys took the ATP Generali Open in Kitzbuehel - his maiden ATP Tour title - edging Alexander Bublik 6-4, 7-6(8-6). Neither event carries ranking weight near the top of the game, and there was no Swiss winner this week.
board.why: First titles are the tour's leading indicator - they mark which unseeded names are about to start troubling the seeds at the bigger hard-court events (Canada, Cincinnati, then the US Open) over the next month.

board.heading: Why it matters
board.title: The Pogačar problem is cycling's success problem
paras: A rider equalling a 40-year-old record should be a celebration; instead the Tour spent three weeks with no genuine general-classification contest, its one plausible challenger (Vingegaard) gone by stage 15. Pogačar himself framed it as "stranger than fiction." The uncomfortable subtext — booing on the roadside, organisers redrawing the Paris finish just to manufacture a stage-winning contest — is that a sport can be dominated so completely that its showpiece loses the very uncertainty that makes it worth watching.

F1's reset went to Mercedes, not the old order. The 2026 rule overhaul was supposed to be a lottery, and it broke against the recent script: Mercedes' second-year driver Antonelli leads by two wins' worth of points, McLaren only won its first race of the year in late July, and the reordered field now includes Hamilton at Ferrari and new entrants filling out the grid. Half a season in, the story is less "who wins in Hungary" than "how permanent is this new hierarchy" — the summer break is the first moment everyone can take stock of it.

board.headline: Van hits Berlin Pride crowd, one killed
board.summary: A van drove into a crowd at Berlin's Christopher Street Day (the city's Pride march) late on Saturday 25 July, killing one person and injuring 16, three of them life-threateningly. The vehicle, a white transporter, struck marchers around 22:00 near Potsdamer Platz in the Tiergarten, and the parade was called off. Berlin police say they identified a fleeing suspect overnight — a 21-year-old man reported by German outlets as Abdul B. — and a citywide manhunt is under way; police describe him as having links to what they call the "Islamist scene," a characterisation that comes from investigators and has not been confirmed by any court or established motive. Of the injured, eight are seriously and five lightly hurt.
board.why: It is the latest in a run of deadly vehicle-ramming attacks in Germany, and both the target — a Pride event — and the still-unproven motive will shape a charged domestic debate over security and extremism; treat the early "Islamist" framing as a police working theory, not a settled fact.

board.headline: Swiss cantons ban 1 August fireworks
board.summary: Several Swiss cantons have issued explicit fireworks bans for the 1 August national holiday as a weeks-long drought keeps most of the country under open-fire restrictions. With near-total bans on open fires already in place across much of Switzerland — Zürich and Winterthur, for instance, prohibit even charcoal grilling in public — cantons have in recent days tightened the rules specifically for fireworks ahead of Saturday 1 August, meaning the traditional displays will be barred almost everywhere.
board.why: It is a concrete, everyday sign of the same European heat-and-drought spell driving the wildfires abroad, and it reshapes how the country's biggest civic holiday will be marked this year.

board.headline: UN warns against wider US-Iran war
board.summary: The UN warned on Friday 24 July against a wider escalation in the US–Iran war and flagged the risk to global shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, as US strikes on Iran paused for a second day. The Strait is the narrow waterway carrying roughly a fifth of the world's oil; the warning came amid renewed Houthi attacks in the Red Sea. US Central Command, meanwhile, says its naval blockade of Iran "remains in force" — so the two-day lull in strikes is a pause, not a settlement, and earlier US framing of a "final" round of strikes has not held up.
board.why: Any closure of Hormuz or spread of the fighting to Red Sea shipping lanes would ripple straight into energy prices and supply chains far from the war zone.

board.headline: Saudi-led coalition strikes Hodeida as Houthis vow response, widening the Gulf war
board.summary: A Saudi-led coalition struck the Houthi-held Yemeni port of Hodeida on Friday 24 July, and the Iran-backed Houthis vowed to retaliate on Saturday 25 July, pulling Saudi Arabia directly into the widening Gulf war. The strikes followed several days of Houthi attacks on Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea; Riyadh said it hit military targets and would "do everything necessary" to protect its shipping against a Houthi-enforced maritime blockade, while the Houthis said the strikes hit civilian infrastructure in Hodeida and injured two people. The flare-up opens a new front alongside the ongoing US-Iran confrontation over the Strait of Hormuz, and the UN warned on 24 July against a wider escalation as fighting intensified around the Red Sea, a corridor that normally carries a large share of world seaborne trade.
board.why: A direct Saudi-Houthi exchange layered on top of the US-Iran war threatens both of the region's two critical maritime chokepoints (Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb) at once, and any sustained closure of Red Sea shipping feeds straight into global energy and freight costs.

board.headline: Three detectors, one ultra-high-energy neutrino puzzle they can't reconcile
board.summary: Ultra-high-energy neutrinos are the most energetic particles known, and three very different instruments have now seen events that don't add up. The balloon experiment ANITA-IV recorded four steep, near-horizon events that look like such neutrinos, and the underwater telescope KM3NeT logged a single record-breaking track — but both imply neutrino rates that IceCube, the largest detector of all, should have seen and did not. The authors build careful energy- and direction-dependent sensitivities for all three and do a joint statistical fit. A steady all-sky neutrino flux fails badly, leaving a ~7.5-sigma tension (sigma measures how many standard deviations the data sit from the model; 5-sigma is the particle-physics discovery threshold, so 7.5-sigma is a serious mismatch); even short transient flares tuned to the observation windows only ease it to ~5.9-sigma. Within the Standard Model, no arrangement of ordinary astrophysical sources reconciles the three datasets.
board.why: a genuine, high-significance puzzle at the energy frontier that points either to new physics or to something the field doesn't yet understand about its own detectors — the kind of anomaly that occasionally reshapes a subfield.

board.headline: Custom RNA drugs cut seizures in two children with a rare genetic epilepsy
board.summary: Two boys, aged 9 and 14, with SCN2A-related developmental and epileptic encephalopathy each received a bespoke antisense oligonucleotide (ASO — a short synthetic genetic strand designed to stick to a chosen RNA and silence it). Each drug was engineered to knock down only the mutated copy of the SCN2A sodium-channel gene while sparing the healthy copy, by targeting single-letter DNA differences unique to the bad allele. Seizures fell by 26% and 90% respectively, medication dropped, neurodevelopment improved, and one child walked independently for the first time — with no drug-related serious adverse events. This is an n-of-1-times-two result, so it is preliminary and needs long follow-up, but the team showed that 16% of a separate SCN2A infant cohort carry differences compatible with the same approach.
board.why: a concrete demonstration that truly individualized genetic medicines can be built and deployed for ultra-rare mutations — with an early hint of how to move from n=1 toward many.
